prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My first week in Cambridge a car full of white boys tried to run me off the road, and spit through the window, open to ask directions. I was always asking directions and always driving: to an Armenian market in Watertown to buy figs and string cheese, apricots, dark spices and olives from barrels, tubes of paste with unreadable Arabic labels. I ate stuffed grape leaves and watched my lips swell in the mirror. The floors of my apartment would never come clean. Whenever I saw other colored people in bookshops, or museums, or cafeterias, I’d gasp, smile shyly, but they’d disappear before I spoke. What would I have said to them? Come with me? Take me home? Are you my mother? No. I sat alone in countless Chinese restaurants eating almond cookies, sipping tea with spoons and spoons of sugar. Popcorn and coffee was dinner. When I fainted from migraine in the grocery store, a Portuguese man above me mouthed: “No breakfast.” He gave me orange juice and chocolate bars. The color red sprang into relief singing Wagner’s Walküre. Entire tribes gyrated and drummed in my head. I learned the samba from a Brazilian man so tiny, so festooned with glitter I was certain that he slept inside a filigreed, Fabergé egg. No one at the door: no salesmen, Mormons, meter readers, exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, no one. Red notes sounding in a grey trolley town.

Nobody ever came knocking: no salesmen, no Mormons, no meter readers, no exterminators, no Harriet Tubman, nobody at all. Red notes ringing out in a drab trolley town.

# A Stranger in Cambridge

When I first arrived in Cambridge, the whiteness of the place struck me before anything else—not the snow, but the faces. As a person of color newly transplanted into this predominantly white world, I felt the sharp edges of racism and the deeper ache of isolation. The stares lingered a moment too long, the conversations stopped a beat too soon, and I learned quickly what it meant to be perceived as an outsider in a city that had never made room for someone like me.

To fill the emptiness, I sought connection in the places that reminded me of home and of everywhere else I longed to belong. I wandered through ethnic markets, running my fingers along unfamiliar packages, breathing in the pungent spices and sweet ferments that crowded the narrow aisles. I immersed myself in the flavors of a dozen cultures—the heat of chilies, the earthiness of unfamiliar roots, the comfort of foods that spoke a language I understood without words. In those moments, surrounded by color and aroma, I could almost forget how alone I was.

But the connections I hungered for most eluded me. Again and again, I tried to reach out to other people of color—a nod, a hesitant smile, the beginning of a sentence. And again and again, these attempts faltered and failed. The words dissolved before they reached my lips, or the moment passed before I could seize it. Each failure left me lonelier than before, uncertain of what to say and doubtful that I would ever find the belonging I sought.

My solitary existence took its toll. I ate poorly, surviving on whatever was cheap and convenient, and my body suffered for it—the exhaustion, the aches, the slow grinding down of a person living without care or company. And yet, even in that bleakness, kindness sometimes appeared where I least expected it. A stranger's small gesture, an unbidden gentleness, would break through the grey and remind me that the world was not entirely cold.

It was in music and dance that I finally found my escape. When the rhythm took hold, something in me came alive that the streets of Cambridge had tried to silence. The sounds bloomed into color, the movement into feeling, and for a while I was no longer an outsider but a body fully present, fully alive. Against the grey and alienating backdrop of my daily life, these vivid moments of sensory abandon stood out like flashes of light—proof that even here, joy was still possible.
outputs.L4:
# Elsewhere, Always

Cambridge in autumn is the color of old parchment—honeyed stone and ivy going rust at the edges, spires reaching into a sky the pale gray of dishwater. I walk its cobbled lanes and understand, in a way that lives beneath language, that this beauty was never built with me in mind.

The first time it happened, I told myself I'd imagined it. A woman clutched her bag closer as I passed on King's Parade, her knuckles whitening, her eyes finding some fascinating point in the middle distance. I catalogued it as coincidence. But coincidence, I've learned, has a rhythm, and I began to hear its steady percussion everywhere: the shopkeeper who followed me between the aisles of the little grocery on Mill Road, the tour guide who paused mid-sentence when I lingered too long near his cluster of listeners, the way conversations in the pub thinned to silence and then resumed in a lower register when I ordered my pint.

I eat alone, mostly. There is a particular loneliness to eating alone in a city of communities—of college formals and rowing clubs and generations of belonging calcified into stone. I have my rituals. On Tuesdays I buy a samosa from the stall near the market and eat it on a bench by the river, watching the punts glide past, the tourists laughing, their reflections trembling in the Cam's brown water. The pastry is warm and spiced and tastes, faintly, of somewhere else—of a home that exists now only in the geography of memory. I press the flavor against my tongue and feel the ache of it, that peculiar homesickness for a place I'm not sure I ever fully possessed.

I have tried to make a map of belonging. I attend the free lectures, sitting in oak-paneled halls beneath portraits of men who would have found my presence unthinkable. I visit the Fitzwilliam Museum on gray afternoons, standing before objects looted from lands like the one my grandparents left, feeling the strange doubling of recognizing myself in the glass cases—displayed, catalogued, admired, but never quite at home. I run my fingers along the spines of books in secondhand shops, breathing in the mildew and dust, searching for a sentence that might explain me to myself.

There are moments of connection, and these are almost worse than the loneliness, because they show me the shape of what I lack. A woman in a café asks about the book I'm reading, and for eleven minutes we talk about everything and nothing, her laughter bright as struck glass. Then her friends arrive, and she turns toward them like a plant toward light, and I become furniture again. A man at the bus stop shares his umbrella during a sudden downpour, our shoulders nearly touching, the rain drumming its intimate percussion above us—and then the bus comes and swallows him and I never see him again. These encounters are like matches struck in a vast dark room: a flare of warmth, a glimpse of a face, and then the returning cold.

The city is beautiful, and its beauty is a kind of cruelty. In the evenings the light goes golden and long, gilding the tops of the colleges, and I walk the Backs where the willows trail their fingers in the water, and I feel the full weight of my apartness settle over me like a second skin. Couples pass, students in gowns, families with their easy laughter—all of them woven into something I can see but cannot enter, a warmth I can press my face against like a child at a lit window in December.

I have been searching, I think, for a moment of arrival—that click of recognition when a place decides to hold you, when the strangeness dissolves and you look up one day to find that you have become part of the pattern. I keep waiting for it. I wait through the changing seasons, through the frost that silvers the grass in the Fens, through the brief and desperate spring. I wait as the tourists come and go and the students graduate and are replaced by other students, an endless procession of belonging that flows around me like water around a stone.

But the arrival never quite comes. Instead there is only this: the accumulation of days, each one bright with sensation and heavy with distance. The taste of cardamom and loneliness. The sound of church bells I do not answer to. The particular quality of light on ancient stone that was placed here, brick by brick, century by century, by hands and for hearts that were nothing like my own.

I am here. I have made myself a life of sorts, stitched together from small observations and smaller kindnesses. And still, some essential part of me remains suspended—forever in the doorway, forever the outsider, forever elsewhere even as I stand exactly, undeniably, here.

# The Armenian Community of Cambridge and Watertown

Nestled in the greater Boston area of Massachusetts, the neighboring communities of Cambridge and Watertown are home to one of the most vibrant Armenian populations in the United States. For over a century, Armenian immigrants and their descendants have shaped the cultural landscape of this region, leaving a lasting legacy that continues to thrive today.

## A History of Settlement

Armenians began settling in the Watertown area in the early 20th century, many of them survivors and refugees fleeing the Armenian Genocide of 1915. Drawn by employment opportunities at local factories, including the Hood Rubber Company, these early immigrants established a foothold that would grow into a flourishing community. Watertown, in particular, became a central hub for Armenian-American life in New England.

## Cultural Institutions and Landmarks

The Armenian presence in Watertown and Cambridge is reflected in numerous cultural and religious institutions. The **Armenian Library and Museum of America (ALMA)**, located in Watertown, houses one of the largest collections of Armenian artifacts outside of Armenia itself, preserving centuries of history, art, and heritage.

Several Armenian churches serve the community, offering not only religious services but also acting as centers for social gatherings, education, and the preservation of tradition. Armenian schools and language programs help pass cultural knowledge to younger generations.

## Food and Everyday Life

Visitors to Watertown can experience Armenian culture firsthand through its many markets, bakeries, and restaurants. Traditional foods such as lahmajoun, kufta, and various pastries can be found throughout the neighborhood, drawing food lovers from across the Boston metropolitan area, including nearby Cambridge with its diverse, academically vibrant population.

## A Lasting Legacy

Today, the connection between Cambridge and Watertown reflects a broader story of immigration, resilience, and cultural preservation. The Armenian community remains an integral part of the region's identity, celebrating its heritage while contributing to the rich, multicultural fabric of Massachusetts.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a young Black woman's isolating first year as a graduate student in Cambridge, Massachusetts, capturing loneliness, racism, and vivid sensory encounters with immigrant communities.
counterfactuals.output:
# First Winter in Cambridge

They told me it would be an honor, this acceptance letter thick as a promise, and so I came north carrying my grandmother's Bible and a coat that would prove useless by November.

---

The cold here has teeth. It bites through the seams of everything I thought I knew about arriving. In seminar I raise my hand and watch how the room rearranges itself around my voice, how the professor's eyes slide past me toward the certainty of other faces. *Interesting,* he says, the way you'd describe weather in a country you'll never visit.

I learn to make myself small in large rooms. I learn the particular silence of being the only one, how it hums beneath fluorescent lights, how it follows me across the quad where the ancient buildings wear their pedigrees like fur coats and I am always, somehow, tracking mud.

---

But listen—

On Prospect Street there is a Haitian bakery where the woman behind the counter calls me *cherie* and the patties come wrapped in paper gone translucent with grease and heat. Here the air is thick with allspice and something like home, though home is six hundred miles south and getting farther. She does not ask what I study. She asks if I am eating. She asks with her whole face.

The Portuguese men outside the market argue over dominoes, their laughter round and rolling, and though I cannot understand the words I understand the shape of belonging when I see it pressed against a folding table.

---

At the Brazilian church I do not attend, I stand outside on Sundays just to hear the singing spill onto Cambridge Street, that gorgeous overflow of praise in a language I taste but cannot speak. The Ethiopian restaurant lets me sit for hours over one cup of coffee, its ceremony slow as mercy, the frankincense curling toward a ceiling stained with decades of other people's exile.

We recognize each other, don't we—we who have come from elsewhere into this cold theater of achievement. We nod. We hold doors. We are fluent in the dialect of *almost.*

---

Some nights I walk the river just to feel the wind confirm what the day already proved: that I am here and not here, present and unaccounted for, a woman rich with citations and poor in the currency of being seen.

The Charles moves black and patient beneath the bridges. The lights of the city I will never quite belong to shimmer on its skin.

I think of my mother's hands. I think of every woman who bent her back so I could sit in rooms that were never built with me in mind.

---

And in the morning, the Dominican man who runs the corner store slides an extra plantain into my bag and says *you look tired, mija, you have to rest,* and I carry that small kindness up four flights of stairs like a coal I am afraid to let go out.

This is how I survive my first winter:

collecting the warmth that strangers leave like breadcrumbs, learning that loneliness and love can share a single street, becoming—slowly, stubbornly—someone who stayed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person autobiographical vignette about being a woman of color newly arrived in a predominantly white New England town, weaving together food, music, migraines, and fleeting connections with strangers.
counterfactuals.output:
The Weather Here

The migraines arrived before I unpacked the last box. My mother would say the pain followed me across three time zones like a stray dog, loyal to my worst self. Here in this town of white clapboard and whiter faces, the light comes in slantwise off the snow, and my skull becomes a cathedral of throbbing.

I press my forehead against the cold window and wait for the aura to pass.

---

At the grocery store I search for the things that would anchor me. No plantains. No proper chilies, only a sad bell pepper the color of an old bruise. The woman at the register has kind eyes and hair like corn silk. She holds up my bag of jasmine rice like it's an artifact.

"Is this the kind you cook in coconut?" she asks.

I don't know what she means, but I nod, because her smile is the first warm thing this week. "Sometimes," I say.

"My son married a girl from Thailand," she offers, as if handing me a coin. I take it. In this economy of strangers, every small offering counts.

---

I cook anyway. I improvise. Cumin I brought in my suitcase, wrapped in a sock so customs wouldn't smell my whole life. The kitchen fills with the ghost of my grandmother's hands, and for a moment the migraine lifts, chased out by memory and steam. I eat standing up, the way I did as a child, licking oil from my fingers while the radio plays.

I found a station that plays the old songs sometimes—late at night, a program hosted by a man with a voice like river stones. Tonight it's a woman singing in a language I half-recognize, the cousin of my mother tongue. I don't understand every word but I understand the ache, and I let it braid itself with mine.

---

The pharmacist knows my name now. This is the intimacy of chronic pain: you become a regular somewhere sterile. He slides the paper bag across the counter and says, "The barometric pressure's dropping. That does it to my wife too."

*That does it to my wife too.*

I want to weep at the ordinariness of it, the way he's folded me into the category of people who deserve gentleness. I am not exotic to him. I am just someone whose head hurts when the storms come.

"Thank you," I say, and mean more than the medicine.

---

On the town green, a girl is busking with a violin, mittens with the fingertips cut off. She is perhaps nineteen, playing something that sounds like longing itself. I drop a bill into her open case. She nods without stopping, and our eyes hold for the length of one long bowstroke.

I think: we are both far from something.

I think: maybe not. Maybe she was born in the yellow house on the corner and has never left. Maybe I am the only exile here, projecting my displacement onto anyone who stands still long enough.

The music follows me home like the migraine did. Some things are kinder to be haunted by.

---

At night the town goes silent in a way my old life never did. No horns, no vendors, no neighbors arguing through thin walls. Just the tick of the radiator and the wind testing the windows. I lie in the dark and press two fingers to my temple, mapping the pain like a country I'm learning.

I am building a life out of small mercies: a cashier's story, a pharmacist's wife, a violinist's glance. Fragments, yes. But my grandmother built our whole family on fragments—a recipe remembered, a song hummed over a sleeping child, a kindness banked against the cold.

Tomorrow I will find the market again. I will ask for the chilies by name, teach them to order what I need. I will let the man with the river-stone voice sing me toward morning.

The snow keeps falling, indifferent and beautiful.

I am still here.

I am learning the weather.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental piece of creative nonfiction that captures alienation and belonging through fragmented images—ethnic markets, Chinese restaurants, samba lessons, and Wagner—narrated by a lonely outsider.
counterfactuals.output:
# Inventory of a Foreign Body

*

The mango sellers know me now, which is to say they don't know me at all. They know the shape of my hesitation, the way I lift each fruit to my nose like I'm listening for something. *Maduro*, the woman says, pressing one into my palm, and I want to tell her that I don't know what ripeness sounds like in any language, that I've been holding fruit up to my face in cities across three continents, waiting for it to teach me how to stay.

*

Consider the Chinese restaurant at 11 p.m. The one with the aquarium in the window, fish circling their small architecture of oxygen and glass. I order in a language I'm still assembling from television and shame. The waiter answers in English. This is the transaction of the almost-belonging: my effort, his mercy, the tea arriving anyway, hot, regardless of what we call it.

*

Fragment: a fortune cookie that read *You will soon cross a great water.* I had already crossed it. I was sitting in its aftermath, in the wet sock of arrival, wondering when the crossing ends and the being-there begins.

*

Samba, Tuesday nights, the community center that smells of floor wax and other people's confidence. *Solta o corpo*, the instructor calls—release the body—and everyone does, hips articulating a grammar I was not raised to speak. My body is a formal letter. My body is a customs declaration. I have nothing to release because I have been holding nothing, only the space where release might live.

*

The others move like water finding its level. I move like water in a photograph of water.

*

There is a specific loneliness to being the only one clapping on the wrong beat. You become the clock everyone tunes against. You become useful, in a way—the negative space that defines the shape of everyone else's rhythm.

*

At home I play Wagner too loud, because Wagner is what my father played, and my father is dead, and the *Liebestod* is the sound of longing that never has to touch its object, that prefers the longing, that would rather ache toward the beloved than survive her. Isolde dies of proximity. I am dying of its opposite. We would have understood each other, she and I, both of us undone by distance—hers too small, mine too large.

*

In the ethnic market—that phrase, *ethnic*, as if some foods are from nowhere, as if some people are just people—I buy things I do not know how to cook. Bitter melon. A root like a knuckled fist. Dried fish that stares. I am building an altar to a homeland that isn't even mine. I am homesick for places I've never been, which is the purest homesickness, unpolluted by memory.

*

Fragment: the cashier and I, watching the total climb, both of us silent, both of us performing the small liturgy of exact change.

*

Question I cannot ask the samba teacher: *When does the body forget it was ever stiff? When does the accent leave? Is there a moment, or only an asymptote, the curve approaching the line it will never touch?*

*

The Chinese restaurant has a photograph by the register: the owner, younger, standing in front of a different restaurant, in a different country, squinting into a sun I will never feel. He crossed his own great water. He is still here, ladling, wiping, circling like the fish. Maybe belonging is not arrival. Maybe belonging is just staying long enough that your foreignness becomes furniture, becomes the aquarium nobody notices anymore, becomes the low hum of the tank.

*

Wagner builds his cathedrals of yearning and never lets them resolve. Four hours, sometimes, before the chord comes home. I have been holding my breath for that chord my whole life. Solta o corpo. Release the body. But into what? Onto whose floor?

*

The mango, when I finally cut it, is perfect. The woman was right. I eat it over the sink, standing, in the country I have moved to, juice on my wrists, and for one animal moment I am not from anywhere and it does not matter. The sweetness asks nothing of my pronunciation. The sweetness is a citizenship no one can revoke.

*

Then the moment passes, as moments do, and I wash my hands, and the water runs, and somewhere Isolde is still dying beautifully, and somewhere a room full of strangers is finding the beat without me, and I stand dripping in the kitchen light—

*

—a foreign body, inventoried, unclaimed, ripe with the particular sweetness of almost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical stream-of-consciousness passage evoking the disorientation of a Black narrator living alone in a "grey trolley town," blending references to Harriet Tubman, Fabergé eggs, and synesthetic color imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Grey Trolley Town

The trolleys pass and I count them by their groaning, one two grey, the rails singing that low iron hymn nobody wrote down—who wrote down Harriet's footsteps, tell me, who transcribed the swamp-water sucking at her heels while she moved north like a rumor, like a color that hadn't been named yet.

I live alone here where the sky is the inside of an oyster, pearl-nothing, and I taste blue when the streetlamp buzzes—did you know sound has a flavor? Mine does. The buzz is cobalt on the tongue, a smear of it, and I press my palm to the window glass and it comes back cold as a Fabergé egg, that jeweled hollow thing, gold-latticed, worth a kingdom and empty at the center, *empty*, imagine building something so precious around nothing, imagine the czars asleep in velvet while somewhere a woman walked eleven times into the mouth of the dark to carry the living out.

I am the living. Am I the living?

Grey on grey the trolley town unspools, and I hear my grandmother's green voice, green like the underside of magnolia, saying *child you got to keep moving*, and Harriet said the same thing didn't she, *keep going*, if you hear the dogs keep going, if you see the torches in the woods keep going, if you're tired keep going, if you want to taste freedom keep going—

but freedom here tastes like the copper of a bitten cheek, tastes like the trolley's third rail, and my rooms are jeweled with nothing, enameled with quiet, and I hold up my hand and it shimmers, brown and gold, a Fabergé thing worth a kingdom, opened, opened, and inside—

—the smell of purple. The color of a train whistle. The long walk North still folded in the marrow.

Two three grey. The trolleys groan. I keep going.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poetic memoir excerpt about solitude, race, and hunger in an unfamiliar city, using surreal and sensory details and ending on an image of red musical notes in a colorless place.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Wednesdays

I arrived in a city that spoke in a language of gray—not the color, but the temperature of its glances. My skin, brown as riverbed clay, became a question no one asked aloud but everyone carried in the corners of their mouths.

Solitude here had texture. It draped over my shoulders like a wet coat I couldn't remove, heavy with the rain of a hundred conversations I wasn't invited into. I walked streets where my footsteps echoed back to me, the only witness to my own existence.

*

Hunger arrived first as sound—a low animal moan from somewhere beneath my ribs. Then it became architecture, building rooms inside me where want could pace and pace. I counted coins the way a priest counts sins: too many, all mine, none redemptive.

The bakery windows fogged with warmth I couldn't afford. Bread rose like small golden suns behind glass, and I pressed my forehead to the cold pane, learning the geometry of denial. My reflection floated there, superimposed over abundance—a ghost hungry for its own life.

*

In this place, I learned that loneliness has a flavor. It tastes like the inside of your own cheek, bitten too many times. It tastes like water when you've convinced yourself it's soup.

The people moved past me in colorless streams. Their faces blurred into the pavement, into the pewter sky, into the aluminum river that cut through the city like a wound that wouldn't scar. Everything drained of pigment. Even my own hands, when I held them up, seemed to fade—as if the city were slowly erasing me, brushstroke by brushstroke.

*

But then—

On a Wednesday shaped like all the others, a woman on a corner opened her mouth and sang.

I did not understand her words. I did not need to.

From between her lips rose notes—actual notes—and they were *red*. Crimson. Arterial. They floated up into the ashen air like embers refusing to die, like poppies blooming in a photograph developed only in silver and shadow. Each note a small rebellion of color, a heartbeat made visible, drifting over the colorless crowd who did not look up, who could not see.

But I saw.

I stood in that gray cathedral of a city and watched red music rise—the only color left in the world, the exact shade of everything I still carried inside me, still burning, still

*alive.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
